8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":17,"verseId":18,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Action and Fruit","totalVerses":33,"verseData":{"id":"v17_18","number":18,"title":"Both Virtuous and Non-Virtuous Karma Persist Until Ripening","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"In this visible world, All actions of the two kinds, Each comprising action and the unexpired separately, Will remain while ripening."},"philosophy":{"insight":"Both categories of karma — virtuous (kuśala) and non-virtuous (akuśala) — along with their nonexpired potential, persist conventionally until ripening. Neither type vanishes prematurely. The karmic \"debt\" (v.14) applies equally to positive and negative actions.","madhyamaka":"Dvividha-karma (two kinds of action): kuśala (virtuous) and akuśala (non-virtuous). Both the karma (action) and the avipraṇāśa (nonexpired potential) persist separately until vipāka (ripening). The action ceases; the potential continues. This distinguishes the deed from its consequence while maintaining conventional continuity.","quantum":"Quantum information conservation: both \"positive\" and \"negative\" quantum states (however defined) are conserved through unitary evolution. Information isn't selectively lost based on its content. Like karma: both virtuous and non-virtuous potentials persist equally.","bridge":"Both quantum information and karmic potential show content-neutral persistence: the system doesn't selectively discard information based on its character. QM: all quantum states are conserved equally. Karma: both good and bad karma persist equally until ripening. Both: persistence is universal, not selective.","accessible":"Both your good deeds and bad deeds \"stay on your record\" until their consequences play out. The universe doesn't preferentially forget bad deeds or remember only good ones. Everything is accounted for — like a comprehensive ledger that tracks all transactions, both credits and debits.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, both types of karma persist and ripen. Ultimately, both are empty. Neither virtuous nor non-virtuous karma has inherent existence — but both function conventionally within the dependent arising of saṃsāra.","commonMisconception":"NOT saying virtuous and non-virtuous karma are morally equivalent. They produce DIFFERENT fruits (pleasant vs. unpleasant). V.18 says they PERSIST equally — both types remain until ripening. Persistence is universal; consequences differ."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Content-Neutral Information Conservation","score":56,"strength":"Medium","explanation":"Quantum information is conserved regardless of content — the system doesn't selectively discard states. Like karma: both virtuous and non-virtuous potentials persist equally until ripening. Persistence is universal.","caveat":"Quantum information conservation is a physical principle. Karmic persistence is a metaphysical/ethical framework. The parallel is about content-neutral persistence."},"animation":{"visualBridge":"Two ledgers side by side: one golden (virtuous karma), one dark (non-virtuous karma). Both remain open until their entries are resolved (ripening). Neither closes prematurely. A scale shows both types persisting equally.","educationalGoal":"User sees that both types of karma persist equally until ripening — no selective forgetting. The karmic system is comprehensive and impartial."},"deeperDive":[{"q":"Why do both types persist equally?","a":"Because karmic persistence is a feature of the SYSTEM (dependent arising), not of the CONTENT (virtuous vs. non-virtuous). The mechanism of karmic continuity is universal — it operates the same way regardless of the action's ethical quality. Just as gravity affects all objects equally regardless of their color.","realLifeExample":"A bank ledger records both deposits and withdrawals equally. The ledger doesn't selectively forget debts or preferentially remember credits. Both are tracked until resolved."},{"q":"What does \"action and the unexpired separately\" mean?","a":"An important distinction: the ACTION (the deed itself) and the UNEXPIRED POTENTIAL (the avipraṇāśa, the karmic \"debt\") are SEPARATE. The action ceases immediately upon completion. The potential persists until ripening. They're distinct but related — like a contract and the obligation it creates.","realLifeExample":"Signing a loan agreement (action) vs. the loan balance (unexpired potential). The signing ceremony is over (action ceased), but the loan balance persists (potential continues) until repaid (ripened)."},{"q":"Does this mean past karma is inescapable?","a":"Not absolutely. V.15 established that wisdom (bhāvanā) can address karmic potential. V.19 will show that nirvana and death provide boundaries. But until these events occur, both types of karma persist. The system is rigorous but not hopeless — liberation is possible.","realLifeExample":"Debts persist until repaid — but bankruptcy (liberation/nirvana) or statute of limitations (death) can provide boundaries. The system is strict but not infinitely oppressive."},{"q":"How does this relate to the promissory note model (v.14)?","a":"V.14 established the model (karma as debt). V.18 specifies that BOTH types of debt (virtuous and non-virtuous) persist. The promissory note model is universal — it applies to all karma, positive and negative. No karmic potential is exempt from the system.","realLifeExample":"A financial system tracks both assets and liabilities. The accounting model applies to everything — credits and debits alike. V.14 established the model; v.18 confirms its universality."},{"q":"What's the significance of \"in this visible world\"?","a":"It specifies that v.18 describes karma functioning within the current cosmic cycle (adṛṣṭa-loka, the \"visible world\" of our experience). This is conventional reality — the world as we experience it, governed by karmic law. It's not a statement about ultimate reality.","realLifeExample":"A company's accounting rules apply \"in this fiscal year\" — within a specific domain of operation. V.18 similarly specifies its domain: the visible world of conventional experience."},{"q":"Why separate \"action\" from \"the unexpired\"?","a":"Because the action CEASES (it's impermanent) while the potential PERSISTS (it's nonexpiring). If they were identical, the action would have to persist permanently (to maintain the potential) or the potential would cease with the action (annihilation). Separating them allows impermanent action with persistent potential — the Middle Way.","deeper":"V.18 adds an important refinement to Nāgārjuna's karma model: the distinction between karma (the action, which ceases) and avipraṇāśa (the nonexpired potential, which persists). This distinction is crucial because it explains how actions can be impermanent (they cease) while their consequences persist (the potential continues). Without this distinction, you face the dilemma of v.6: permanent action or no consequence. With it: impermanent action + persistent potential = Middle Way."}],"quiz":{"beginner":{"question":"Do virtuous and non-virtuous karma persist equally?","options":["A) Only bad karma persists","B) Yes — both types persist equally until ripening.
